why: People write step-by-step instructions so that someone else can do a task.
how: Children write the steps for a task, such as washing hands, so a younger child can follow them.

why: A good set of steps starts from thinking about the person who will follow it.
how: Children put picture cards of a kind act in order and act them out.

why: A daily routine written as steps shows how many people help at each one.
how: Children draw three steps of their morning with the helper at each step.

why: Building a sequence one block at a time gives each child an equal share of the making.
how: Pairs build a ScratchJr program by adding one block each in turn.

why: When the order is wrong the program fails, and putting it right takes another try.
how: Children run a mixed-up sequence, swap one block and run it again until it works.

why: Giving and following instructions in order needs two people working closely.
how: One child gives instructions in order and the other follows them exactly, then they swap.

why: A loop repeats the same small effort until the goal is reached.
how: Children use a Repeat block to move a character a little each time until it arrives, and tell the story of not giving up.

why: A repeating pattern made by two people only works if they keep in step.
how: Pairs invent a three-move dance, perform it as a loop, then program it with a Repeat block.

why: Some good actions are worth repeating every day.
how: Children name a thank-you they say every day and program a character to say it in a loop.

why: An event block invites the question of what will set the program going.
how: Children guess what starts a program with a new start block, then try it and see.

why: A character can be programmed to respond when someone needs it.
how: Children program a character so that when it is tapped it goes to help another character.

why: What happens after a bump is a choice, in a program and in the playground.
how: Children program what a character does when it is bumped, such as saying sorry.

why: An if-then rule applies the same way to everyone, which is what makes it fair.
how: Children act out if-then cards about sharing and check the rule works for every child.

why: Noticing how someone feels is the 'if' that leads to a kind 'then'.
how: Children play an if-then game, choosing a kind action for each feeling card.

why: A true answer to the 'if' question is needed for the rule to work.
how: Children practise answering if-then questions truthfully about their own work.

why: Changing a stored value and watching what happens invites the question 'what if?'.
how: Children guess, change the number on a block and run the program to see.

why: A value that stores whose turn it is helps everyone share fairly.
how: A card on the table records how many turns each child has had with the tablet.

why: A stored value is only useful if it is the real one.
how: Children record a game score exactly as it is, even when they are behind.

why: Finding the step that fails and fixing it means trying again with a plan.
how: Children find the block that does not work, change it and run again, counting their tries with pride.

why: Fixing a bug starts with saying plainly what went wrong.
how: In a closing circle children finish the sentence 'My bug was... and I fixed it by...'.

why: A classmate whose program fails needs encouragement before advice.
how: When a partner's program fails, children say one encouraging thing before suggesting a fix.

why: Testing only works if you report what actually happened.
how: Children predict what a program will do, run it and report truthfully whether they were right.

why: A test is a way of finding out something you do not know yet.
how: Children run a program, ask 'what if', change one block and test their idea.

why: One test is rarely enough, so testing means coming back to it.
how: After a fix, children run the program three more times to be sure it still works.

why: A big job feels possible when it is done one small part at a time.
how: Children split a project into three parts on paper and tick each one off as it is built.

why: Once a job is split into parts, each person can take one.
how: Pairs divide a project so each child builds one part, then join the parts together.

why: Big things are made of many parts, each done by someone.
how: Children list the parts of a school day and thank the person behind one of them.

why: Finding a pattern begins with noticing what is the same and what is different.
how: Children guess a hidden sorting rule and test the guess with new objects.

why: A sorting rule can leave something out, and a fair rule has a place for everything.
how: Children sort objects by a rule, find one that does not fit and change the rule.

why: A pattern is only useful if we describe what we really see.
how: Children describe an object's features exactly before deciding where it goes.

why: Two programmers on one project succeed only by planning and working together.
how: One child handles the tablet while the other directs, and they swap every five minutes.

why: A shared tablet needs fair turns.
how: Pairs use a timer so each child has the same time in control.

why: Helping a partner well means leaving them able to do it themselves.
how: Helpers point and ask questions but keep their hands off the partner's tablet.

why: Finishing a project is the moment to thank the people who helped.
how: Children end a project with a page or recording that thanks those who helped them.

why: Looking at a classmate's work is a chance to find the good in it and say so.
how: Each child tells a partner one kind and true thing about their project.

why: A project can be made for someone else's enjoyment.
how: Each child chooses a real person to make a project for and shows it to them.
